name: Kira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at the Tarrow iron ore mine, the big P&H with a bucket you could park two cars in. My job is loading the haul trucks, three passes a truck, and I'm the senior shovel operator, so I set the dig plan with the shift supervisor and train the new operators. I love the rhythm of it, swing, dump, swing, and when the truck drivers line up nice and tight I can do forty trucks an hour. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights and the drive back to Pellow at 7 in the morning with the sun in my eyes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a house on Ridge Road in Pellow with two girls from the processing plant. I'm single, which suits me for now. Money's tight because Tarrow pays under the industry rate and I'm helping my little brother through his apprenticeship, buying his tools and half his rent. I've got maybe ten days of money saved, so I'm not exactly a role model.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of a let-down, to be honest. I use this stuff every day and I was kind of hoping it'd go somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, which it was, but the useful bits are still useful. I'd tell people at work to at least try the tools, because they help with the boring stuff. Online I'd probably post something like, so the robots aren't coming, back to fighting for a pay rise then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd been learning the remote shovel system on the side because I thought that was my way out of nights. If nothing changes, I'm in the same cab with the same pay for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI to plan dig sequences on paper and to study the remote operations manuals, because it's still faster than doing it myself. I'd keep at the shovel and push the union to close the pay gap with the other iron ore mines. And I'd keep paying for my brother until he finishes next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly bored by it. Relief and disappointment at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI for, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All sorts. I ask it to explain the hydraulics fault codes, I get it to quiz me on the remote operator modules, I even used it to write my brother's tool list. Last month it helped me work out a better bench sequence and the supervisor actually used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a role model with money. What would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my brother finishing his apprenticeship. That's three hundred a week back in my pocket. Until then I'm living paycheck to paycheck and I've made peace with it, because he'd do the same for me.

S0.say: It was oversold, but the useful bits are still useful, so try the tools. Online I'd say the robots aren't coming, so back to fighting for a pay rise.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd been learning the remote shovel system as my way out of nights. If nothing changes, I'm in the same cab on the same pay for twenty years.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily to plan dig sequences and study remote-operation manuals, stays on the shovel, and backs the union push to close the pay gap. Keeps paying for her brother's apprenticeship until he finishes next year.
S0.feel: Calm, a little bored, with relief and disappointment mixed together.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm in the same cab with the same pay for twenty years.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is the rare miner who finds the no-change picture a let-down; she'd been treating automation as her way out of night shifts. She already uses AI for real work, and her supervisor adopted one of her plans. Her thin savings come from supporting her brother, which she accepts without complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I've been preparing for. Tarrow already runs two of the drills from the operations centre in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to get people off nights and out of the dust, but only if workers get the new jobs, not just new contractors. I'd want the union to sign a deal that every remote seat goes to someone already on site first. I'd post that and I'd say it at every crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do well out of this. I already know half the remote system and I'm the senior on shovels, so I'm the obvious pick for the first remote seat. What bugs me is that most of my crew won't be, and I'd feel a bit like I'm climbing over them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the remote operator role the day it's posted, probably in the city ops centre, three hours from Pellow. I'd offer to run lunch sessions for anyone on my crew who wants to learn the system. And I'd push for the union to make paid training part of the deal, not something you do at your kitchen table like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. With a guilty edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move three hours away. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent in the city's double what I pay in Pellow, so the first few months would be ugly, with ten days of savings. I'd probably sleep on my cousin's couch for a bit. And I'd miss the girls in the house and football on Saturdays, but I'd come back on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said climbing over your crew. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, mainly. He's been on the shovel thirty years and he taught me half of what I know. He won't touch a laptop. If I get the seat and he gets a payout, I'll feel like I took his job with the skills he gave me.

S1.say: This is a chance to get people off nights and out of the dust, but only if workers get the new jobs. Every remote seat should go to someone already on site first.
S1.think: I'd do well, because I know half the remote system and I'm the senior shovel operator. What bugs me is that most of my crew won't, and I'd feel like I'm climbing over them.
S1.do: Applies for a remote operator seat at the city operations centre the day it's posted, sleeping on a cousin's couch at first. Runs lunch sessions to teach her crew the system and pushes the union for paid training.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a guilty edge about colleagues left behind.
S1.quote: If I get the seat and he gets a payout, I'll feel like I took his job with the skills he gave me.
S1.fieldNote: Kira sees steady disruption as her opening, and she's clearly ahead of most of her crew. Her guilt about her mentor Rob is the emotional centre of the scenario. She pairs her own move with a demand that workers on site get first claim on new roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's different. If AI can do almost anything, then the remote seat goes too. My whole plan is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, and I mean properly, like the mines being taxed per robot and the money going to the towns. I'd be at the protests and I'd be one of the loud ones online. A mine is a hole in public land, the ore belongs to everyone, so the profit from robots digging it should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared, more than I'd want anyone to see. I'm the one who's always said this tech is exciting, and in two years it takes everything I've built. With ten days of savings I can't sit around waiting for a policy to pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after any job installing or fixing the robots, because for a year or two someone has to set them up, and I'd move to wherever that is. I'd tell my brother he's on his own for rent, which would kill me. I'd cut everything else and use the AI tools to learn robotics maintenance as fast as I can, nights, weekends, whatever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I can move, I'm 27, I'm single, I'm quick. But it's a race, and I'd not be sure I'd win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I chase the setup jobs and nothing else. There's no time to build a career, just to grab the next six-month contract. It'd feel like jumping from one moving truck to another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the ore belongs to everyone. Who do you blame if this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shareholders, and the governments that let them write the rules. Not the engineers, not the tech, they're just doing their jobs. If the profits stay with ten people in a boardroom, that's a choice, not a law of nature.

S2.say: The gains have to be shared, like taxing mines per robot and giving the money to towns. The ore belongs to everyone, so the profit from robots digging it should too.
S2.think: I'd be more scared than I'd let anyone see. I've always said this tech is exciting, and in two years it takes everything I've built, with ten days of savings.
S2.do: Chases short contracts installing and fixing robots wherever they are, moving as needed. Stops paying her brother's rent, cuts all extra spending, and uses AI tools to cram robotics maintenance on nights and weekends while joining protests.
S2.feel: Anxious but still mobile; it feels like a race she might not win.
S2.quote: It'd feel like jumping from one moving truck to another.
S2.fieldNote: The plan she'd built for steady change collapses in this picture, and she says so right away. Her youth, single status and comfort with tools keep her from alarm, but thin savings make it a race. She blames shareholders and governments, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to be ahead of it, I think. Not safe, but ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns the robots, and that's the only question that matters. I'd push the union to ask for a share of the automation savings in the next agreement. And I'd tell everyone under 35 to start learning the systems now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I could have three or four good years as a remote operator or automation tech before it all goes fully self-running. That's enough to save something for once. After that I genuinely don't know, and I'd be lying if I said I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd take the remote seat and do a part-time certificate in industrial automation, online, using AI to study. I'd move to the city by year two once my brother's finished. I'd also join the party branch in Pellow, because five years is enough time for a law about robot taxes if people push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the background, but I'd be busy enough not to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with two, actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish what I've started. My brother finishes, I get the certificate, I save. With two years everything's a scramble, with five it's a plan with a cliff at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a cliff at the end. What's at the bottom of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. Maybe some kind of public income, maybe jobs we can't imagine yet. I'd rather be one of the people deciding what's down there than one of the people falling.

S3.say: We have five years to decide who owns the robots, and that's the only question that matters. Everyone under 35 should start learning the systems now.
S3.think: I could get three or four good years as a remote operator or automation tech and finally save something. After that I genuinely don't know.
S3.do: Takes the remote seat in year one while studying an online automation certificate with AI help, and moves to the city in year two once her brother finishes. Joins a local party branch to push for a robot tax.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background, but busy enough not to dwell on it.
S3.quote: With two years everything's a scramble, with five it's a plan with a cliff at the end.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her time to finish obligations to her brother and build a qualification. She is honest that she can't see beyond 2031. Her politics turn into a concrete step: joining a party branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 37. That's a lot of time if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, and if we don't, it's because someone chose not to. I'd want public training funds, union seats on the automation boards, and the robot tax. I'd say that loudly and often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd have time to become an automation engineer, maybe even get the degree I never did. The scary thing isn't me, it's Pellow, because a town of shovel operators doesn't retrain itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote seat, finish the automation certificate in two years, and then go for an engineering degree part-time while working. I'd keep running the lunch sessions for my crew. And I'd save, properly, for the first time in my life, maybe a hundred a week once my brother's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. It's the only one where I feel like the time is on my side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Pellow need, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training centre in town, not three hours away. And some new business that isn't the mine, maybe repairing the robots for all the mines in the region. If you could keep the jobs local, the town keeps its football club and its school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd feel guilty about Rob. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In ten years Rob retires anyway, he's 58. He'd go out on his own terms. That actually makes me feel better than anything else in this picture.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this fairly, and if we don't, someone chose not to. We need public training funds, union seats on automation boards and a robot tax.
S4.think: I'd be fine, maybe better than fine, with time for an engineering degree. The scary part isn't me, it's Pellow, because a town of shovel operators doesn't retrain itself.
S4.do: Takes the remote seat, finishes an automation certificate within two years, then starts a part-time engineering degree. Keeps teaching her crew and saves around a hundred a week once her brother finishes.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful; time feels on her side.
S4.quote: The scary thing isn't me, it's Pellow, because a town of shovel operators doesn't retrain itself.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Kira's worry shifts from herself to her town. She imagines a local repair hub serving the region's robots. Her relief that her mentor Rob could retire on his own terms shows how much her guilt drove earlier answers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where being quick doesn't save you. What would help is a payment from the robot tax straight to the people in mining towns, and paid training while you look for the next thing. Not a loan, a payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd want the robots, and the answer is yes, if we own a bit of them. Nobody grows up dreaming of twelve-hour nights in a shovel cab. I'd hand that over tomorrow if the money came with it.

headlineQuote: Nobody grows up dreaming of twelve-hour nights in a shovel cab. I'd hand that over tomorrow if the money came with it.
portrait: Kira Quinn is a 27-year-old senior shovel operator at an iron ore mine, single, sharing a house, and supporting her younger brother through his apprenticeship on ten days of savings. She uses AI tools every day and has been teaching herself the remote-operation system as a way out of night shifts. She's calm in the plateau and steady pictures, though guilty about colleagues like her mentor Rob. Two-year AGI makes her anxious and sends her chasing robot setup contracts, while five and ten years let her plan a certificate, a degree and a move. Her politics centre on who owns the robots and whether mining towns share the gains.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the only picture where being quick doesn't save her.
whatWouldHelp: A payment from a robot tax going straight to people in mining towns, plus paid training while they look for the next job.
